The response bias parameter c reflects the decision threshold adopted by an individual, which may depend on factors such as expectations and potential consequences of the decision, and it can be estimated as

In the context of the truth effect, many theories predict a more liberal decision threshold (i.e., a smaller value of c) for repeated compared to new statements, for instance, due to increased fluency or familiarity (Speckmann & Unkelbach, 2022; Unkelbach, 2007).

In line with this expectation, the estimated effect of repetition on c was -0.40 (SE = 0.05) in our empirical example (see Table 2). When modeling truth judgments, the parameter d ′ depends on an individual's prior knowledge, such that individuals with greater domain knowledge can better distinguish between true (signal) and false (noise) statements.

In our example in Table 2, the intercept for d ′ was 0.16 (SE = 0.04), meaning that the means of the noise and signal distributions were separated by 0.16 standard deviations (i.e., probit units) on average. It is often assumed that repetition does not affect the ability to discriminate between true and false statements, which is in line with the non-significant effect of repetition on d ′ in Table 2 (but see Fazio et al., 2015; Schmidt & Heck, 2026).

The two-step SDT estimation approach comes with several limitations. First, reliable estimation of sensitivity (d ′ ) and decision criterion (c) per person requires a sufficient number of trials in each condition, which may be impractical in many settings (Levine et al., 2022). Second, by requiring aggregated response frequencies across items for hierarchical SDT models using probabilistic programming languages such as JAGS or Stan (e.g., Lee & Wagenmakers, 2014; Paulewicz & Blaut, 2020; Rouder et al., 2007). However, this can be time-consuming and error-prone for researchers without specialized expertise.

each person, the two-step SDT approach neglects inherent item-level variability, which can result in biased parameter estimates (Morey et al., 2008; Rouder & Lu, 2005; Rouder et al., 2007). Third, the reliance on z-transformations in the two-step SDT approach renders the parameter estimates highly sensitive to extreme values. For instance, perfect discrimination (i.e., a hit rate of 1 and a false alarm rate of 0) produces an infinite d ′ value and a non-identified c parameter, because the data are not informative regarding response biases.

Although certain corrections are available (e.g., N. A. Macmillan & Kaplan, 1985), they depend on arbitrary adjustments which affect d ′ and c. This can introduce biases and reduce statistical power through data exclusion (Brown & White, 2005), possibly leading to distortions and increased Type I and Type II error rates (Chen et al., 2024). Robust estimation methods for d ′ and c have been proposed (e.g., Hautus, 1995; Verde et al., 2006), yet the accuracy of these estimates depends heavily on sample size, irrespective of the specific method (Miller, 1996). These issues become more relevant when including more factors, since choice frequencies need to be computed based on a smaller number of observations (i.e., for each cell of the factorial design). Thus, the probability of obtaining extreme and missing values increases.

Generalized Linear Mixed Models

Generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) extend traditional regression models for non-normally distributed dependent variables (Bates et al., 2015; Pinheiro & Bates, 2000).

GLMMs model binary judgments at the trial-level and assume that each response follows a

Bernoulli distribution (or equivalently, a binomial distribution with only one observation).

While fixed effects account for the effects of experimental factors or covariates, the inclusion of random effects enables modeling dependencies stemming from different sources (e.g., from persons and items). The probability of observing an affirmative response (e.g., judging a statement as "true") in a crossed design, with each item j being judged once by each person i, is formally expressed as

The function g(•) is the probit or logit link function, while g -1 (•) is the inverse link function which transforms the unbounded, linear predictor term into a probability in the range from zero to one. Regarding the parameters, γ 0 is the fixed intercept across all items and persons, which corresponds to the grand mean if all predictors are centered. Moreover, u 0,i represents subject-specific deviations (random intercept per person) and v 0,j item-specific deviations (random intercept per statement). The predictor variables are included in the matrix X, with X ij referring to the row for item j and person i, and are modeled by the regression coefficients in the vector β ij . If all or some of these coefficients are assumed to be constant across items and persons, a GLMM with fixed slopes is specified. Alternatively, random effects of the regression coefficients can be included to account for differences in slopes between subjects and items:

While the fixed-effects parameters in the vector γ correspond to the average slopes at the latent probit or logit scale, the item-and person-specific deviations in the vectors u i and v j are assumed to follow centered multivariate normal distributions. Separate multivariate distributions are assumed for all person random effects (i.e., u 0,i and u i ) and all item random effects (v 0,j and v j ). The corresponding two covariance matrices, which determine the variances and correlations of random-effects, are estimated as free parameters (for details, see Bates et al., 2015). To test whether a fixed effect differs significantly from zero, statistical inference is typically based on the Wald z-test, which is default output in most software for mixed-models with nonlinear link functions (e.g., lme4; Bates et al., 2015).

Each estimated coefficient is divided by its standard error to yield a z-statistic, which is compared against the standard normal distribution to obtain a p-value.

The mixed-effects framework is particularly valuable for fully crossed experimental designs, where variation exists across subjects and items (Epifania et al., 2024; Singmann & Kellen, 2019). Accounting for both sources of variance is especially relevant in areas with qualitative differences between stimuli such as the truth effect, where statements differ in plausibility, syntactic complexity, and difficulty (Aktepe & Heck, 2025). Thereby, GLMMs address a critical limitation of methods requiring an aggregation of binary judgments either across items within person (as in F1 ANOVA and two-step SDT) or across persons within item (as in F2 ANOVA; Baayen et al., 2008; Bates et al., 2015). The GLMM approach also circumvents scale distortions introduced when fitting nonlinear models to aggregated data (Estes, 1956).

GLMMs naturally accommodate unbalanced designs and missing responses without requiring data imputation (Baayen et al., 2008; Pinheiro & Bates, 2000). Moreover, GLMMs automatically implement partial pooling and shrinkage. Partial pooling refers to using information from the group to inform parameter estimates at the individual level, which reduces the variance in parameter estimates (Quené & van den Bergh, 2008). This results in shrinkage, meaning that extreme estimates are systematically pulled towards the overall mean, preventing overfitting and yielding more reliable estimates (McElreath, 2018).

GLMMs can be specified in a manner to implement SDT within a mixed-effects framework, allowing researchers to focus on discrimination ability and response bias while accounting for complex dependencies. For this purpose, it is necessary to model binary judgments by a GLMM with a probit link function, g(p) = Φ -1 (p), while including the actual status of the items as a contrast-coded predictor (+0.5 = "true," -0.5 = "false;" for tutorials, see Samara, 2026; Zloteanu & Vuorre, 2024). As a result, the estimated intercept corresponds to the negative response bias (-c) in SDT, while the estimated coefficient for the actual item status corresponds to the discrimination ability parameter d ′ (DeCarlo, 1998; Rouder & Lu, 2005). Intuitively, this is due to the fact that a larger intercept generally results in a higher predicted probability of responding "true," whereas a larger slope for truth status results in a larger difference in the response probabilities for true and false statements. The effect of other factors (e.g., repetition) on the response bias c can be modeled by including main effects in the matrix X (e.g., a column with +0.5 = repeated, -0.5 = new). A positive main effect of repetition means that repeated statements are more likely to receive "true" responses overall, corresponding to a lower c (i.e., a more liberal criterion) for repeated than for new statements. This is exactly the result in our empirical example in Table 2, where the estimate for the repetition effect is already multiplied by -1 to facilitate interpretation in terms of c. The estimate -0.40 (SE = 0.05) is very similar to the one from the two-step SDT approach. While additive effects correspond to effects on c, multiplicative interaction terms with item status can be included to test whether factors moderate the discrimination ability d ′ . For instance, a positive repetition-status interaction term would indicate that repetition improves discrimination between true and false statements. In our empirical example in Table 2, this interaction was not significant.

Random effects in GLMMs also carry substantive interpretation within the SDT framework. Random intercepts for subjects and items reflect subject-and item-specific differences in the response criterion (c). Random slopes for repetition by subject capture person-specific differences in the strength of the repetition effect on the response bias c.

Similarly, random slopes for truth status reflect subject variability in sensitivity (d ′ ), indicating that discrimination ability differs rather than being fixed at the population level.

By adding random slopes of the repetition-status interaction for subjects, one can account for subject-specific variation in the effect of repetition on d ′.

Despite offering many advantages, GLMMs also come with practical challenges.

Their estimation can be computationally costly and prone to singular fits, especially when assuming complex random effects structures (Barr et al., 2013; Jaeger et al., 2011).

Bayesian mixed models are less prone to convergence and singularity issues and may allow stable estimation of more complex hierarchical structures (Bürkner, 2017; Gelman et al., 2020). Irrespective of whether mixed models are fitted in a frequentist or Bayesian way (for a comparison, see Dalla Bona et al., 2026), specifying the optimal random effects structure remains contentious, with ongoing debates over whether "maximal" models (Barr et al., 2013) or parsimonious models (Bates et al., 2018; Matuschek et al., 2017) are better at balancing Type I error and statistical power. Maximal GLMMs account for all possible sources of variance in a study (e.g., persons and items) by including corresponding random intercepts and random slopes for all predictor variables. Such models can be empirically unidentifiable when there is insufficient data to estimate their parameters, in turn requiring a very large number of observations for convergence and non-singular fits (Jaeger et al., 2011). In contrast, parsimonious models include random slopes only for some predictors and some sources of variance based on prior knowledge and theoretical considerations, which facilitates model fitting. We explain the specification and interpretation of different random-effects structures for factorial designs in the next section. Note that the selection of which fixed effects to include in a GLMM is beyond the scope of this paper, as we assume that all experimental factors and their interactions are of interest, and thus included in all model versions (for guidance, see Bates et al., 2015; Kuznetsova et al., 2017).

Since GLMMs for binary data lack a residual variance, their coefficients cannot easily be converted into standardized effect sizes such as Cohen's d. As a remedy, interpretation can be facilitated by computing marginal means, which are predicted means for certain conditions averaged over all other factors in the model (Lenth, 2023). The computation of the coefficient of determination (R² ) in GLMMs is also more intricate than in ANOVA due to the inclusion of random-effect variances, the lack of an explicit residual variance of the binomial distribution, and the non-linear link function. Nakagawa and Schielzeth (2013) proposed two types of R² for mixed models: marginal R² m , which quantifies the proportion of variance explained by the fixed effects only, and conditional R² c , which represents the proportion of variance explained by both the fixed and random effects (see also Johnson, 2014). However, for singular models (i.e., if one or more random-effect variance components are estimated to be zero or are not identifiable), conditional R² c cannot be computed, as the random-effect structure does not contribute meaningfully to the model variance (Bates et al., 2015; Nakagawa et al., 2017).

Reanalyses of Truth Effect Datasets

Our comparison resembles recent multiverse analyses which have been proposed for studying the robustness of results against using different methods (Harder, 2020; Steegen et al., 2016). Specifically, we study whether and how results differ in terms of p-values and parameter estimates, as well as regarding tests of assumptions, singular fits, and model selection indices. Standard effect sizes are not directly comparable between ANOVA and GLMMs, which estimate marginal effects on observed proportions and conditional effects on a latent probit scale without a residual variance, respectively. We therefore compare ANOVA and GLMMs via hypothesis tests, and compare parameter estimates only between two-step SDT and GLMMs, which share the same latent scale.

Eligibility Criteria for Dataset Selection

Figure 2 shows the PRISMA-like procedure (Page et al., 2021) we used to systematically select openly available datasets of studies investigating the repetition-based truth effect. We first identified papers citing the seminal work on the truth effect by Hasher et al. (1977). Citation records were retrieved from Google Scholar (Haddaway et al., 2015).

Two student assistants screened all papers citing Hasher et al. (1977), working backwards in time from 2024 and stopping in 2009, well before the earliest study with openly available data. Hence, the number of records was not fixed in advance. The assistants screened non-overlapping sets of publication years, so interrater reliability could not be computed; instead, the first author checked all classifications.

Titles and abstracts of all papers were screened for relevance regarding the truth effect. Papers and reported studies not directly related to the phenomenon were excluded, yielding a total of 235 studies. ANOVA was used in 141 studies, mixed models in 41 studies, and two-step SDT in 4 studies (with some studies using multiple methods; see supplementary materials for details).

The remaining studies were screened based on four criteria. First, only studies with openly accessible datasets were included, reducing the sample to 135 studies between 2018 and 2024. Figure 3 shows the number of truth effect studies per year since 2009. Note that none of the studies before 2017 shared their data publicly. Second, we selected datasets that included binary judgments, leaving 46 datasets. Third, 16 studies that met the first two criteria had to be excluded because their datasets could not be reformatted for the reanalysis as the available data contained only aggregated response frequencies (rather Studies screened by title and abstract for relevance to the truth effect (N = 235) Peer-reviewed articles: N = 182 Unpublished theses: N = 31 Conference papers: N = 1 Preprints: N = 21 Studies with openly accessible datasets (published 2018-2024) (N = 135) Datasets including binary judgments (N = 46) Datasets reformattable for reanalysis (raw judgments and codebook available) (N = 30) Studies included in final analysis (repetition and truth-status information available) (N = 20) Excluded: dataset not openly accessible (N = 100) Excluded: judgments not binary (N = 89) Excluded: aggregated data only or no codebook (N = 16) than raw judgments) or due to lacking code books, resulting in a total of 30 datasets.

Finally, we excluded 10 studies that did not contain information about repetition or the truth status of the presented statements, which is required for SDT. Table 3 provides an overview of the 20 studies remaining for the reanalysis, featuring N = 3, 318 subjects and N obs = 212, 555 observations in total.

Analysis Workflows

All datasets were first preprocessed to have long format (i.e., one judgment per row). We preserved all observations as made available by the original authors and did not apply any additional data cleaning.

RM-ANOVA of choice proportions.

Separate ANOVAs were fitted for the F1 and F2 analyses using the afex package (v1.3-1; Singmann et al., 2015). In both analyses, the dependent variable was the proportion of "true" responses (p true ), while the independent variables comprised repetition, the truth status of the statements, and other study-specific categorical variables, along with all interactions. Repetition was specified as a repeated-measures effect in both ANOVAs (i.e., within subjects or within items), while truth status was a within-subject effect in F1 but a between-item effect in F2 ANOVA. The other variables were adjusted based on the specific experimental design of the studies.

The Greenhouse-Geisser correction was automatically applied to adjust the degrees of freedom in the case of sphericity violations. The Shapiro-Wilk test was used to assess whether residuals were normally distributed, and Levene's test was employed to assess the homogeneity of error variances, both using the performance package (v0.12.2; Lüdecke et al., 2021).

Two-step SDT approach.

For the two-step SDT workflow, we computed hit and false alarm rates per subject, which were then plugged into Equations ( 5) and ( 6) to obtain measures of discrimination ability (d ′ ) and response bias (c) for new and repeated statements (Batailler et al., 2022). Extreme cases with hit or false alarm rates equal to 0 or 1 were corrected by adjusting the values to 1/(2N obs ) and 1 -1/(2N obs ), respectively, where N obs is the number of observations in a cell of the factorial design (N. A. Macmillan & Kaplan, 1985). If a correction was not possible and one or more missing indices were obtained, the subject was entirely excluded from the transformed dataset.

We conducted two separate repeated-measures ANOVAs for d ′ and c, each with repetition as independent variable to statistically assess the effect of repetition on discrimination ability and response bias. Repetition was contrast-coded using sum-to-zero coding (new = -0.5; repeated = 0.5). Models were fitted using the lmer function from the lme4 package (v1.1-35.5; Bates et al., 2015), employing a linear mixed-effects model with random intercepts for subjects. Finally, p-values were computed using Satterthwaite's approximation for the degrees of freedom, as implemented in the lmerTest package (v3.1-3; Kuznetsova et al., 2017).

GLMMs.

In the GLMM workflow, binary truth judgments were modeled using repetition, truth status, other study-specific factors, and all interactions as independent variables. All factors were dichotomous and coded with sum-to-zero contrasts, with one level assigned a value of -0.5 and the other 0.5. Thereby, the corresponding coefficients can directly be interpreted as the effect of the manipulation.

Models were fitted using the glmer function from the lme4 package (Bates et al., 2015) using a probit link function. Estimating GLMMs can be difficult because they often suffer from issues such as singular fits or converge issues. To address these problems, we explored alternative optimization algorithms for maximum-likelihood estimation. The default optimizer was nloptwrap in lme4's glmer function, but we additionally experimented with bobyqa, Nelder-Mead and nlminb algorithms from the optimx package (v2023-10.21) to make sure that all models were estimated properly and converged (Nash & Varadhan, 2011). As the final numerical optimization method, we used the nlminb optimizer as it showed the fewest singularity issues across all datasets and model versions.

Note, however, that the optimizer may need to be adjusted for other datasets, as no single optimizer is universally optimal. A singular fit means that the estimated covariance matrix of the random effects is not of full rank, for instance, because a variance is estimated to be zero or a correlation to be ±1 (Bates et al., 2015 (Bates et al., , 2018)). For each GLMM, we recorded whether the fit was singular using the function isSingular in lme4. All percentages reported below refer to the proportion of non-singular fits.

The random-effects structures specified in the models are presented below using lme4 syntax (Bates et al., 2015). For readers unfamiliar with this notation, the expressions Model selection among GLMM versions was conducted using Akaike and Bayesian information criteria (AIC and BIC; Akaike, 1974; Schwarz, 1978). Besides, to assess the proportion of explained variance, marginal R² m values, which measure the variance explained only by fixed effects, and conditional R² c values, which measure the variance explained by both fixed and random effects, were computed for each GLMM version (Johnson, 2014; Nakagawa & Schielzeth, 2013) using the r2_nakagawa function in the performance package (Lüdecke et al., 2021). All datasets and R scripts for analysis are available at the Open Science Framework (OSF) repository (https://osf.io/eh7tn/).

Results of the Reanalyses

Because the ground truth is unknown for empirical data, the reanalyses focus on the agreement between methods rather than on their performance, which we evaluate in the simulation study below.

Comparison of F1, F2, and min-F ′ ANOVA

To assess whether the effect of repetition generalizes not only across persons but also across statements, we compared the number of significant test results when evaluating the main effects and interactions of all factors in a study using either F1 ANOVA (aggregation across items) or F2 ANOVA (aggregation across subjects), or the min-F ′ statistic. Figure 4 illustrates the extent to which p-values differed between these analyses. To facilitate an assessment of both non-significant and significant p-values, the first row of panels shows p-values at the probability scale, whereas the second row uses a log scale. Out of 192 tested effects, 10 were significant only in the F1 but not in the F2 ANOVA, while three were significant only in the F2 but not in the F1 ANOVA. Aside from these minor discrepancies in statistical significance, the overall pattern remained largely consistent across F1 and F2 ANOVA, regarding both raw p-values (r = .89, 95% CI: [.85, .91] p < .001) and log p-values (r = .71, 95% CI: [.64, .78] p < .001), which shows that the results did not substantially differ between the two types of analysis. Figures regarding the repetition, status and repetition-status interaction only can be found in the supplementary materials.

Overall, 48 effects remained significant across all three analyses, although min-F ′ produced noticeably larger p-values. Additionally, 10 effects that were significant in both the F1 and the F2 ANOVA were no longer significant with the min-F ′ statistic (seven of these non-significant effects involved the factor repetition and its interaction with other factors). These findings indicate that the min-F ′ test statistic is more conservative, which results in reduced statistical power for detecting significant effects.

To evaluate the degree to which effects explain a similar amount of variance across items and across persons, we compared the coefficient of determination (R² ) obtained from the F1 and F2 ANOVA. We observed that in 6 datasets, R² values were larger for the F1 analysis, whereas in 14 datasets, R² values were larger for the F2 analysis. The average amount of explained variance was similar for F1 ANOVA (R² = .25, SD = .20) and F2 ANOVA (R² = .29, SD = .31). These results indicate that the explained variance attributable to item-level differences cannot be neglected. Moreover, Pearson's correlation analysis indicated a significant positive correlation between R² values of the F1 and F2 analyses (r = .58, 95% CI = [.19, .82], p < .001). Because F1 and F2 analyses aggregate judgments either by subject or by item, respectively, the results should be interpreted with caution. The results do not imply the superiority of one analysis over the other, but rather highlight the relevance of differences between statements while providing evidence for the robustness of conclusions.

Finally, ANOVA relies on several statistical assumptions, including homogeneous error variances, which is typically assessed using Levene's test, and normally distributed residuals, evaluated using the Shapiro-Wilk test. The results of Levene's test indicated that the assumption of homogeneity of variances was met in all datasets for F1 ANOVA and in 90% of the datasets for F2 ANOVA. However, the Shapiro-Wilk test revealed that the normality assumption was satisfied only in 15% of the datasets for F1 ANOVA and 70% for F2 ANOVA. These findings suggest that using choice proportions as the dependent variable in ANOVA frequently violates the normality assumption, particularly in studies with small sample sizes.

Results of GLMMs

We observed notable differences in the proportion of non-singular fits across random-effects structures (Table 4). The models with random intercepts only (RI and 2RI) and the model with random slopes for repetition for subjects and random intercepts for items (RS) resulted in non-singular fits in 100% of the datasets. The model with random slopes for repetition and status for subjects and random intercepts for items (RSS), which was selected most often by AIC (see below), and the model with random slopes for repetition for both subjects and items (2RS) were non-singular in 75% of the datasets. In contrast, the most complex model (3RS), despite being theoretically desirable (Barr et al., 2013), was non-singular in only 55% of the datasets, even in those with a large number of observations. The model with complex random intercepts (CRI) was non-singular in only 25% of the datasets.

We determined the most appropriate random-effects structure by comparing GLMMs with varying specifications using AIC and BIC, considering only non-singular fits.

According to AIC, the best-performing model in 9 datasets assumed random slopes for repetition and truth status for subjects (RSS), but only random intercepts for items. The most complex model (3RS) was selected in 4 datasets, and this model had the smallest mean AIC across all datasets, closely followed by RSS (mean ∆AIC = 2.24; (Table 4). The model with random slopes for repetition for subjects and random intercepts for items (RS) was selected in 5 datasets, and the model with random slopes for repetition for both subjects and items (2RS) in 2 datasets.

BIC results differed slightly, favoring the model with random slopes for repetition for subjects and random intercepts for items (RS) in 9 datasets. The second-best model, selected in 8 datasets, included random slopes for both repetition and status for subjects, and random intercepts for items (RSS), which had the smallest mean BIC across all datasets (Table 4). Additionally, the model with random intercepts for both subjects and items (2RI) was preferred in 2 datasets, while the model with random slopes for repetition for both subjects and items (2RS) was optimal only in 1 dataset (see supplementary materials for the dataset-specific values). Overall, the model selection results provide clear empirical support for including random slopes of repetition for subjects, while there was more ambiguity regarding the inclusion of random slopes for the other factors. The model with random intercepts and slopes of repetition and status for subjects and random intercepts for items (RSS) was selected both by AIC and BIC in 6 datasets, and the model with random slopes of repetition for subjects and and random intercepts for items (RS) in 4 datasets. In one dataset, the model with random intercepts and slopes of repetition for both subjects and items (2RS) was selected by both AIC and BIC. There was no other agreement between AIC and BIC for any other model in the datasets. Table 4 also shows R² for all GLMM versions. Conditional R² c values, which reflect variance explained by both fixed and random effects, were substantially larger than marginal R² m values, indicating that subject-and item-level variability accounted for a considerable proportion of variance. As expected, both conditional and marginal R² values increased with model complexity in each dataset. Note that the average values in Table 4 do not strictly follow this ordering, because conditional R² c could not be computed for models with singular fits or convergence failures and was thus excluded. For example, although the complex random intercepts model (CRI) has the highest R² values, the computed values are from only a very small subset of the datasets, as CRI resulted in singular fits in most datasets. Overall, differences in R² among GLMM specifications were small, both overall and within individual datasets (see supplementary materials). The estimated size of the repetition effect was very similar across GLMM versions.

The mean of the probit coefficients ranged from 0.262 (Range: [-0.034, 0.589]) in the random intercepts for subjects only model to 0.297 (Range: [-0.043, 0.698]) in the most complex model. Parameter means and ranges were almost identical in those models including at least one random slope term. More generally, all estimated coefficients (including repetition) were very similar across GLMM versions, with mean probit values ranging from 0.072 (Range: [-1.593, 1.336]) in the random intercepts for subjects only model to 0.076 (Range: [-1.820, 1.414]) in the model with random slopes for repetition for subjects and random intercepts for items. The mean of the estimated coefficients increased slightly from the simplest model (0.072) to the model with random slopes for repetition for subjects and random intercepts for items (0.076). However, further increases in model complexity (i.e., adding multiple random slopes) did not change the fixed-effect estimates on average, which remained within a very narrow range (0.075 -0.076). Comparison of the two-step SDT approach and GLMM estimates

Figure 6 compares the fixed-effects estimates of the two-step SDT approach and the GLMM with random intercepts and slopes of repetition for subjects, and random intercepts for items (RS model). Most of the estimates were closely aligned between the two methods. Where the estimates differed, the GLMM yielded estimates of larger magnitude for discrimination ability d ′ (i.e., the main effect of truth status) and, in several datasets, for the effect of repetition on the response bias c. This is in line with the advantage of GLMMs that they model item variability directly instead of aggregating judgments across items, which attenuates SDT estimates in the two-step approach (Morey et al., 2008; Rouder et al., 2007). Moreover, in one dataset (i.e., Nadarevic et al., 2021 Study 3), the two-step SDT approach resulted in an extreme estimate of the effect of repetition on discrimination ability (about -1.3), whereas the GLMM yielded an estimate close to zero. However, as we do not know the ground truth, it is not possible to conclude which model is more accurate. As a remedy, we performed a simulation study.

Simulation Study

The simulation study evaluated the performance of the different methods for binary judgments for data with a fully crossed, mixed factorial design with participants and items as crossed random factors. We generated datasets mimicking typical truth-effect studies in our reanalysis, in which participants judge the truth of new and repeated statements that are either true or false. The simulation was run using the SimDesign package (v2. 25 Chalmers & Adkins, 2020), with R code and results being available at the OSF repository.

The simulation used a full factorial design with four factors: number of subjects (50 or 100), number of items (40 or 80), true effect size of repetition (0 or 0.3), and true effect size of the repetition-status interaction (0 or -0.3), yielding 16 simulation conditions. In each condition, 5,000 datasets were generated, where each subject responded to each item exactly once (a fully crossed subject-by-item design), with item order randomized independently per subject. Item status (true vs. false) was fixed at the item level: the first -1.5 -1.0 -0.5 0.0 0.5 1.0 1.5 -1.5 -1.0 -0.5 0.0 0.5 1.0 1.5 Two-step SDT vs. GLMM Two-step SDT Estimates GLMM Estimates Parameter Intercept (c) Repetition Status (d') Rep:Status Note. The random effect-effect structure of the GLMM was: (1 + repetition | subject) + (1 | item). Error bars correspond to 95% confidence intervals.

half of items (by index) were assigned "true" and the remaining half "false", so status did not vary across subjects for a given item. Repetition (new vs. repeated) was manipulated within subjects and balanced within each status category, such that each subject received an equal number of new and repeated true statements, and an equal number of new and repeated false statements. Binary responses were generated from the GLMM version with the most complex random-effects structure (3RS), described in the Reanalyses section, where Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution function.

The predictors repetition and status were sum-to-zero contrast-coded (+0.5 and -0.5), and responses were drawn from a Bernoulli distribution using a probit link function.

All data-generating parameters are summarized in Table 5. The fixed-effect coefficients played two different roles in the simulation: The effects of interests were determined by the design factors (repetition: β1 =0 or 0.3; interaction: β3 = 0 or -0.3), allowing us to directly assess Type I error and power for the effects targeted by the analysis. The non-manipulated parameters, the intercept (β 0 ) and the status effect (β 2 ), were not fixed at specific values but drawn independently for each simulated dataset from uniform distributions bracketing empirically plausible values.

All simulation values were determined based on the average and ranges of parameter estimates in the reanalyses of truth-effect datasets (see supplementary materials for details). This was done so that the conclusions generalize across a plausible range observed in prior model fits to real data.

Subjects were assigned correlated random intercepts and random slopes for repetition and status (u 0i , u 1i , u 2i ), and items were assigned correlated random intercepts and random slopes for repetition (v 0j , v 1j ). Items did not receive a random slope for status because status is a between-item factor. Subject and item random effects were drawn from a three-and a two-dimensional normal distribution, respectively. For each simulated dataset, standard deviations and correlations of these random effects were independently sampled from uniform ranges (similarly as in Barr et al., 2013) centered on mean parameter values obtained from our empirical reanalysis, and the resulting correlation matrices were converted to covariance matrices. Since independent random sampling of pairwise correlations does not guarantee that the three-dimensional covariance matrix is positive semi-definite, each generated matrix was checked via eigendecomposition 4 and, where necessary, corrected to the nearest positive-definite matrix before random effects were drawn from a multivariate normal distribution. Finally, to emulate realistic data loss, a random proportion of responses between 0% and 5% was set to missing (completely at random) in each simulated dataset.

Results of the Simulation Study

We fitted the same models described in the Reanalyses section to each dataset generated in the simulation. The most complex model (3RS) corresponds to the true, data-generating model whereas all other, less complex GLMM versions make incorrect, simplifying assumptions regarding the random-effects structure. Non-singular fits were most common for the intercepts-only models (RI and 2RI; above 99.9%), followed by the models with random slopes for subjects only (RS: 92.5%; RSS: 53.2%). Non-singular fits were least common for the more complex models 2RS, 3RS and CRI with 50.9%, 29.0% and 7.7%, respectively. 5 Unless stated otherwise, Type I error rates, power, bias, and RMSE were computed across all replications, including singular fits. Only in the model selection analyses with AIC and BIC, we additionally report results after excluding singular fits.

Figure 7 presents Type I error rates for the main effect of repetition and the repetition-status interaction across the four sample-size combinations. For the main effect, models based solely on random intercepts (RI and 2RI) and the by-items F2 ANOVA showed severe inflation (.162 -.315), worsening markedly as the number of items increased, while min-F ′ was overly conservative throughout (.013 -.026). In contrast, F1 ANOVA remained close to the nominal level for the main effect (.057 -.074). For the interaction, the pattern shifted, such that F1 ANOVA became the most inflated test (.080 -.126), 4 Covariance matrices for subject random effects were positive definite in 80.04% of generated datasets. 5 The normality assumption was met in 46.4% of the datasets for F1 ANOVA and in 85.8% for F2 ANOVA. increasing with the number of subjects, whereas F2 ANOVA showed more moderate inflation (.054 -.075) and GLMMs with random intercepts only (RI and 2RI) showed somewhat reduced, though still high error rates (.070 -.112) relative to the main effect.

Min-F ′ statistics remained markedly conservative for the interaction as well (.006 -.015).

Across both effects, GLMMs with random slopes of repetition for both subjects and items (2RS) plus random slopes of status for subjects (3RS) consistently produced error rates closest to the nominal α level (main effect: .057 -.063; interaction: .054 -.062), showing minimal sensitivity to sample size. GLMMs with complex random intercepts (CRI) also remained reasonably well calibrated across both effects (main effect: .069 -.076; interaction: .059 -.070). In contrast, GLMMs with random slopes for subjects only (RS and RSS) were anti-conservative, more strongly so for the interaction (.074 -.100) than for the main effect of repetition (.066 -.080), with Type I error rates increasing with the number of subjects. The two-step SDT approach showed a similar inflation (main effect: .064 -.081; interaction: .072 -.099).

The reason is that these methods do not account for item-specific deviations in the repetition effect (i.e., the random slope v 1j of repetition for items). Since truth status is a between-item factor, the repetition-status interaction is estimated by comparing the repetition effect between the sets of true and false items.

Hence, item-specific variability in the repetition effect directly adds to the sampling variability of the interaction estimate. Ignoring this variance component (as in RS, RSS, F1 ANOVA, and the two-step SDT approach) results in standard errors that are too small and, in turn, in inflated Type I error rates, especially when the number of subjects is large relative to the number of items.

Since 2RS, 3RS, and CRI resulted in singular fits most often, one might suspect that their good calibration depends on whether the fit was singular. To check this directly, we computed Type I error rates separately for non-singular and singular fits. For 2RS and 3RS, Type I error rates based only on non-singular fits were at or slightly below the nominal level (main effect: .043 -.062; interaction: .044 -.052), whereas singular fits had slightly higher rates (main effect: .060 -.066; interaction: .058 -.069). Thus, the good calibration of these models is not an artifact of selecting non-singular fits. Instead, singular fits of 2RS and 3RS were slightly anti-conservative, but still much closer to the nominal level than RS and RSS, whose Type I error rates were similarly inflated for non-singular fits (main effect: .060 -.078; interaction: .072 -.101).

Figure 8 shows that for the main effect, power increased primarily with number of subjects (e.g., F1 ANOVA: .829 -.875 with 50 subjects to .959 -.976 with 100 subjects), and the random-intercepts-only models (RI, 2RI) and F2 ANOVA showed the highest power (.943 -.999), though this reflects their inflated Type I error rather than genuine sensitivity. For the interaction, power ranged from .275 (min-F ′ , smallest sample) to .992 (RSS, largest sample). Unlike the main effect, RS and RSS showed the highest power for the interaction (.634 -.992), slightly exceeding RI and 2RI (.612 -.985) and clearly exceeding F1 and F2 (.582 -.983), while min-F ′ again showed markedly the lowest power.

The two-step SDT approach also showed comparable power with the GLMMs (.634 -.986). The models with the best-calibrated Type I error (2RS, 3RS, and CRI) showed power for the interaction (.608 -.981) comparable to, though marginally lower than, RS and RSS, indicating that stricter control over Type I error did not come at a substantial cost to power once the number of subjects reached 100. Note that the higher power of RS and RSS for the interaction partly reflects their inflated Type I error rates. As for Type I error rates, power was computed across all replications, including singular fits, which occurred most often for 2RS, 3RS, and CRI. Overall, this should be considered when weighing these models' suitability to specific applications, since high singularity rate limits the practical applicability of otherwise well-calibrated models in real datasets with comparable sample sizes.

We also investigated model selection of GLMM versions using AIC and BIC. The most complex 3RS model was the true data-generating model, so selection of other GLMMs means that simpler models achieve comparable statistical performance for the given sample sizes. We first conducted model comparisons after excluding singular fits. The results showed that the RS model was the winning model in 32.8% of the simulated datasets according to AIC, followed by RSS (28.7%) and 3RS (13.2%).

For BIC, RS was again the winning model most often, in 47.1% of the simulated datasets, followed by 2RI (26.3%) and RSS (19.6%). We repeated the analysis while including all models regardless of whether the fit was singular. (37.3% of the simulated datasets), followed by 3RS (28.9%) and RS (15.9%). According to BIC, RS was still the winning model most often (38.8%), followed by RSS (26.4%) and 2RI (23.3%). We also examined how often a given model was selected by both AIC and BIC simultaneously. Figure 9 shows that, when singular fits were excluded, RS was the joint winner most often, being selected by both indices in 21,050 of the simulated datasets, considerably more than any other model. When singular fits were included, RSS became the most frequent joint winner (12,962 datasets), followed by RS (9,796 datasets).

Figure 9

Confusion matrices of how many times AIC and BIC selected a specific GLMM version. Figure B1 in Appendix B shows the average bias of the fixed-effect estimates, that is, the mean deviation of the estimated parameters from their true simulation values.

Overall, bias was unaffected by the number of participants and items. Therefore, we report bias averaged across the four sample-size conditions. When the true effects of repetition and the interaction were zero, all models were essentially unbiased (absolute bias below .005). If the effects were nonzero, the GLMM with random intercepts for subjects only (RI) showed the largest bias, underestimating the magnitude of the repetition (-0.032) and interaction effects (0.033 for a true effect of -0.3). It was followed by the GLMM with random intercepts for subjects and items (2RI; -0.012 and 0.013) and the two-step SDT approach (2S-SDT; -0.008 and 0.006). In contrast, the GLMMs with random slopes and complex random intercepts (RS, RSS, 2RS, 3RS, and CRI) were close to unbiased (absolute bias of about .004 or less). The same ordering emerged for the non-manipulated fixed-effects parameters (intercept and status), with RI underestimating the status effect (i.e., d ′ ) most strongly (-0.055), followed by 2RI (-0.023) and 2S-SDT (-0.013).

Because bias does not capture the variability of estimates, we additionally examined the root mean squared error (RMSE) of the fixed-effect estimates (Figure B2 in Appendix B). RMSE was affected mainly by the design and only to a small degree by the model version. For all parameters, RMSE decreased with more participants and more items, whereas differences between models within a design cell were small (typically below .01 for the intercept, repetition, and interaction). Doubling the number of items had the strongest effect on the non-manipulated parameters of intercept and status estimates, whereas doubling the number of participants had a larger effect on the repetition estimates.

For the interaction, both factors reduced RMSE substantially. The random-slope models, which were nearly unbiased, yielded almost indistinguishable RMSE values that were slightly higher than those of the simpler models. RI and 2RI often had the lowest RMSE for the intercept, repetition, and interaction despite their larger bias. This advantage was most pronounced when the true effect was zero, where all models were practically unbiased, indicating that the simpler models produce less variable estimates. For nonzero effects, this advantage diminished as bias increased. In the largest design (100 participants, 80 items), RI had the highest RMSE for both the repetition and interaction estimates. For status, RI performed clearly worst with 80 items. The two-step SDT approach (2S-SDT) achieved RMSE values comparable to those of 2RI and was among the lowest for the non-manipulated intercept and status effects, but ranked between the random intercepts only (RI and 2RI) and more complex models (3RS and CRI) for the manipulated repetition and interaction effects.

Discussion

We compared analysis approaches for binary judgments that differ in terms of aggregation level and analytic focus: repeated-measures ANOVA of choice proportions, two-step SDT, and GLMMs of dichotomous responses. Besides discussing their theoretical assumptions and practical implementation, we compared these approaches empirically using a multiverse analysis (Steegen et al., 2016) by reanalyzing 20 truth effect studies with openly available data. We complemented our reanalysis of real data with a simulation study in order to provide practical guidance for analyzing binary judgments in psychological research.

In the reanalyses, the truth effect was robust, and the overall pattern of p-values was similar across methods. F1 and F2 ANOVA yielded highly correlated p-values, whereas min-F ′ was more conservative: Of the 58 effects that were significant in both F1 and F2 ANOVA, ten (17.2%) were not significant for min-F ′ , seven of which involved repetition.

GLMMs with random intercepts only yielded markedly smaller p-values than F1 ANOVA, whereas adding random slopes of repetition for subjects yielded comparable p-values.

Adding further random slopes changed p-values, fixed-effect estimates, and explained variance only slightly, but frequently resulted in singular fits (3RS: 45% and CRI: 75% of the datasets). Accordingly, AIC and BIC mostly selected models with random slopes for subjects but only random intercepts for items (RS and RSS).

The simulation showed that methods ignoring major sources of random variance were anti-conservative. F2 ANOVA and GLMMs with random intercepts only (RI and 2RI) showed inflated Type I error rates for the main effect of repetition, which varied mainly across subjects. F1 ANOVA, the two-step SDT approach, and GLMMs with random slopes for subjects only (RS and RSS) showed inflated Type I error rates for the repetition-status interaction (up to .126, .099, and .100, respectively), because they ignore item-specific variability of the repetition effect. GLMMs with random slopes of repetition for both subjects and items (2RS and 3RS) kept Type I error rates closest to the nominal level, whereas min-F ′ was overly conservative and had the lowest power. As in the reanalyses, these more complex GLMM versions frequently showed singular fits and were rarely selected by AIC and BIC. These results qualify the common arguments against aggregated analyses. Although the normality assumption was frequently violated in the reanalyses, F1 ANOVA kept Type I error rates close to the nominal level for the main effect of repetition, in line with the robustness of ANOVA for dichotomous data (Lunney, 1970). The main limitation of F1 ANOVA and the two-step SDT approach was rather that they ignore item variability, just as F2 ANOVA ignores subject variability, whereas combining both via min-F ′ ensures generalizability only at the cost of power (Richter, 2006). Hence, the main advantage of GLMMs is not that they resolve violations of distributional assumptions, but that they account for random variability across subjects and items simultaneously.

Regarding the random-effects structure of GLMMs, both studies showed that random slopes of repetition for subjects are essential, which provides converging evidence with previous studies showing pronounced interindividual differences in the truth effect (Schnuerch et al., 2021; Zajdler & Schnuerch, 2026). The role of random slopes for items is less obvious, since corresponding GLMM versions were rarely selected by AIC and BIC and often resulted in singular fits. However, omitting random slopes for items inflated Type I error rates for the interaction in the simulation study. This apparent contradiction is resolved by the assumed size of the item variance. The standard deviation of the random slopes of repetition for items was small (σ v1 ≤ 0.27, compared to σ u 1 up to 0.92 for subjects). Such a small variance component improves the likelihood only slightly, which is easily outweighed by the penalty of AIC and BIC, and it is often estimated to be zero (resulting in a singular fit). Nevertheless, assuming random slopes for items matters for testing the interaction of repetition and the between-item factor truth status, which is estimated by comparing repetition effects between the sets of true and false items. Thus, model selection by AIC or BIC does not protect against inflated Type I error rates.

Similarly, the small item variance is consistent with the hypothesis that repetition increases perceived truth to a similar degree for all statements (Fazio et al., 2019, but see Aktepe and Heck, 2025), but it does not imply that random slopes for items can be omitted without consequences for statistical inference. Singular fits were therefore a practical rather than an inferential problem of the design-based models. In the simulation, Type I error rates of singular fits of 2RS and 3RS were only slightly higher than those of non-singular fits and still much closer to the nominal level than those of RS and RSS (see supplementary materials). GLMMs with complex random intercepts (Scandola & Tidoni, 2024) were also reasonably well calibrated, but resulted in singular fits most often.

When estimating SDT parameters, GLMMs with random slopes were practically unbiased, whereas the two-step SDT approach and GLMMs with random intercepts underestimated the magnitude of the effects at a comparable RMSE. This bias partly reflects that ignoring random variability on the latent probit scale, either by aggregating across items or by omitting random slopes, attenuates the estimates toward marginal effects, similarly as for the difference between marginal and conditional effects noted in the Reanalyses section. The larger GLMM estimates of d ′ and of the repetition effect on c in the reanalyses are in line with this attenuation of two-step SDT estimates.

Based on our reanalysis and the simulation study, we recommend the following strategy for confirmatory hypothesis tests of binary judgments in crossed designs. First, statistical methods should account for the main sources of random variance, that is, for subjects and items simultaneously. F1 ANOVA, F2 ANOVA, and the two-step SDT approach do not meet this criterion, and min-F ′ has very low power. Second, the random-effects structure of a GLMM should match the design, with random slopes for subjects for all within-subject factors and random slopes for items for all within-item factors (in truth-effect studies, the 3RS model). Theoretical considerations and prior knowledge can help to identify the most relevant variance components, such as interindividual differences in the repetition effect. Third, if such a complex model results in a singular fit, it can be simplified step by step, for instance, by first removing correlations and then variance components close to zero (Bates et al., 2018; Matuschek et al., 2017), possibly guided by AIC and BIC. However, a singular fit alone is not a strong reason to remove random slopes for items, and researchers should be aware that omitting random slopes for within-item factors can inflate Type I error rates for interactions of such factors with between-item factors (up to about .10 in our simulation). The final random-effects structure and whether the fit was singular should be reported. Fourth, SDT parameters should be estimated with probit GLMMs rather than with the two-step SDT approach.

Similar random-effects specifications can serve as a starting point when studying other psychological phenomena involving binary judgments.

Several limitations need to be considered. The data-generating model in our simulation was the 3RS GLMM, which favors GLMMs, and this model in particular, by construction. Moreover, all design factors had only two levels, so that the performance of the methods may differ for other data-generating mechanisms and more complex designs.

Our results may also not generalize to fields with larger item variability, such as psycholinguistics, where experimental materials cover only a small subset of the possible linguistic units (Baayen et al., 2008). Moreover, we focused on frequentist methods, and future studies could investigate whether Bayesian mixed models also benefit from simpler random-effects structures.

Our study was also limited to binary judgments and did not include Likert ratings, which are ideally modeled using ordinal regression such as cumulative-link mixed models (Bürkner & Vuorre, 2019), an approach used only by very few truth-effect studies (e.g., Henderson et al., 2021). Due to our focus on SDT, we did not consider alternative link functions such as the logit link (Luce, 2005), even though the choice of link function can affect the presence and size of certain effects (Aktepe & Heck, 2025). Finally, we did not consider cognitive models such as evidence accumulation models (Pan & Hu, 2025) and multinomial processing tree models (Fazio et al., 2015; Schmidt & Heck, 2026), which decompose binary judgments into latent processes but rely on stronger assumptions and are computationally more demanding, especially as hierarchical models (Heck et al., 2018).

Conclusion

We compared widely used aggregated and trial-level statistical approaches for binary judgments in within-subject designs: repeated-measures ANOVA, a two-step SDT approach, and GLMMs, which automatically provide SDT estimates for discrimination ability and response bias when using a probit link function. Our reanalyses of 20 openly available datasets on the repetition-based truth effect and a simulation study showed that methods ignoring the random variability of either subjects or items can result in inflated Type I error rates, whereas min-F ′ is overly conservative. GLMMs account for differences between individuals and between items simultaneously. Compared to the two-step SDT approach, GLMMs estimate discrimination ability and response bias with less bias, without requiring aggregation or corrections for extreme proportions. GLMMs with a random-effects structure matching the design kept Type I error rates closest to the nominal level, but frequently resulted in singular fits, whereas simpler GLMMs with random slopes for subjects only were favored by AIC and BIC at the cost of inflated Type I error rates for interactions. Overall, our findings highlight the benefits of GLMMs for binary judgments, with a random-effects structure that is based on the design and simplified only if necessary, while taking into account the consequences of such simplifications for hypothesis tests. 40 items 50 subjects 100 subjects RI 2RI RS RSS 2RS 3RS CRI 2S-SDT RI 2RI RS RSS 2RS 3RS CRI 2S-SDT 0.06 0.07 0.08 0.09 0.10 0.07 0.08 0.09 0.10 0.08 0.10 0.12 0.14 0.08 0.10 0.12 0.14 0.06 0.07 0.08 0.10 0.11 0.12 0.13 0.14 0.15 RMSE 80 items 50 subjects 100 subjects Repetition (true = 0) Repetition (true = 0.3) Interaction (true = 0) Interaction (true = -0.3) Intercept Status RI 2RI RS RSS 2RS 3RS CRI 2S-SDT RI 2RI RS RSS 2RS 3RS CRI 2S-SDT 0.06 0.07 0.08 0.09 0.10 0.07 0.08 0.09 0.10 0.08 0.10 0.12 0.14 0.08 0.10 0.12 0.14 0.06 0.07 0.08 0.10 0.11 0.12 0.13 0.14 0.15

( 1 |

subject) indicates that the model includes random intercepts for subjects (i.e., allowing the overall response level to vary between subjects). Similarly, (1 | item) adds random intercepts for items. Adding predictors inside the parentheses, such as (1 + repetition | subject), means that both the intercept and the slope of the factor repetition are allowed to vary across subjects, thereby capturing individual differences in how repetition affects judgments. When multiple random terms are combined, as in (1 + repetition | subject) + (1 | item), the model accounts for random variation in both subjects and items.3 Furthermore, the colon : denotes an interaction between grouping factors, e.g., (1 | subject:repetition) denoting a unique intercept for each subject-repetition combination. The slash, / in (1 | subject/repetition:status) expands to a nested grouping structure, so it includes subject-level random intercepts along with random intercepts for each subject-repetition-status combination (for more details seeBates et al., 2015; Scandola & Tidoni, 2024). In our GLMM reanalyses, the following random-effects structures were fitted for each dataset: 1. RI model: (1 | subject), specifying random intercepts for subjects only; 2.2RI model: (1 | subject) + (1 | item), specifying random intercepts for subjects and items; 3. RS model:(1 + repetition | subject) + (1 | item), specifying random intercepts and slopes for repetition for subjects, and random intercepts for items; 4. RSS model: (1 + repetition + status | subject) + (1 | item), specifying random intercepts and slopes for repetition and status for subjects, and random intercepts for items; 5.2RS model: (1 + repetition | subject) + (1 + repetition | item), specifying random intercepts and slopes for repetition for both subjects and items; 6.3RS model: (1 + repetition + status | subject) + (1 + repetition | item), specifying random intercepts and slopes for repetition and status for subjects, and random intercepts and slopes for repetition for items; 3 All models specified here allow for correlated random intercepts and slopes. To specify models with uncorrelated random effects, researchers can use a double pipe (||) instead of a single pipe (|) in the model formula.7. CRI model (complex random intercepts; Scandola & Tidoni, 2024): item/repetition), specifying random intercepts for subjects and items, as well as random intercepts for each combination of subject and repetition, subject and truth status, subject, repetition, and truth status, and item and repetition.

Comparison of GLMMs and F1 ANOVAFigure5shows p-values and log p-values for F1 ANOVA and the GLMM versions (plots showing only the effects of repetition, truth status, and their interaction can be found in the supplementary materials). The model including only random intercepts for subjects resulted in smaller p-values. Adding random intercepts for items did not address this issue.
